builder_plan.scenario: Your self-hosted model spends too long generating answers token by token.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a compatible draft model and serving integration exist before renting compute.
builder_plan.baseline: The same target with speculation off, then your existing drafter if you have one.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted draft length, tokens per second, tail latency, output quality, and total GPU cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding
summary: Replaces a neural draft model (e.g., TinyLlama) in speculative decoding with a CPU-based memory classifier that predicts the next token from a four-token window, using no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. Cost is a domain-matched memory model that must be built per domain, sub-millisecond CPU inference, and acceptance rates (38.1% on legal text) well below neural drafters, which limits gains when the verifier is already KV-cached. It can fail on out-of-domain text where the memory classifier's acceptance collapses, and the energy-optimal draft length differs from the speed-optimal one, so naive configuration can raise energy without improving throughput.
rationale: The reader has exactly the constrained setup the paper targets (consumer GPU, energy sensitivity), but the modest 1.25x gain under realistic KV-cached serving and the domain-dependence of acceptance require validation on their own workload before adoption.

claims.statement: Replaces a neural draft model (e.g., TinyLlama) in speculative decoding with a CPU-based memory classifier that predicts the next token from a four-token window, using no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. Cost is a domain-matched memory model that must be built per domain, sub-millisecond CPU inference, and acceptance rates (38.1% on legal text) well below neural drafters, which limits gains when the verifier is already KV-cached. It can fail on out-of-domain text where the memory classifier's acceptance collapses, and the energy-optimal draft length differs from the speed-optimal one, so naive configuration can raise energy without improving throughput.

With a KV-cached verifier, Olifant yields 1.25x throughput and the lowest energy in the study (93 J per 100 tokens); without KV cache, 2.43x throughput and 2.51x lower energy per token on domain-matched EU legal text.
